analysis.one_liner: Repeals the fracking exemption from the Safe Drinking Water Act and requires public disclosure of fracturing chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote, despite 73 cosponsors, and died when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would remove the special exemption that oil and gas drilling received in 2005, which allows companies to inject fracturing fluids underground without following the Safe Drinking Water Act rules that other underground injection must follow. It would also require drilling companies to tell the state what chemicals they plan to pump into the ground before they start, report what they actually used afterward, and make that information public. If a worker or resident is exposed and a doctor needs to know the chemicals, the company would have to hand over the formula immediately, trade secret or not.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking operations and drink the water: they would finally be able to see which chemicals are being injected under or near their homes, and doctors treating suspected exposures could get the chemical identities without waiting for company permission.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents and workers near fracking sites

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Safe Drinking Water Act exemption for hydraulic fracturing, bringing those injections under the same underground injection controls as other drilling-related injections.

Requires operators to disclose, before and after each job, the chemicals used — including chemical constituents, CAS numbers, safety data sheets, and volumes — and requires states to post that information publicly online.

Requires immediate disclosure of proprietary formulas or trade secret chemical identities to a treating physician or nurse during a medical emergency, even before any confidentiality agreement is signed.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas drilling companies and their chemical suppliers, who would face new federal oversight, paperwork, and public reporting, and would lose the confidentiality of many chemical formulas from the public record.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers and chemical suppliers

drawbacks.text: Drillers and chemical makers would face real compliance costs: tracking and reporting every chemical and volume for every well, and having state agencies publish it online, adds expense and administrative burden to operations.

The bill erodes trade secret protection for chemical formulas by requiring disclosure to states and doctors in emergencies, which companies argue exposes proprietary blends they spend money developing; the bill does preserve a carve-out barring public disclosure of proprietary formulas outside the emergency-disclosure pathway.
Opponents of federal oversight argue that states closer to the wells are better positioned to regulate the industry, and that a new federal permitting layer could slow energy production.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is large for the people most affected: communities sitting on top of fracking operations currently cannot find out what is being injected near their water, and the bill's emergency-disclosure rule is aimed squarely at that gap. The costs fall on a specific, profitable industry in the form of reporting and oversight. The honest trade-off question is whether federal Safe Drinking Water Act oversight is heavier than needed — but the bill is narrowly written, leaving routine natural gas storage exempt and protecting ordinary proprietary formulas from blanket public disclosure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Environment and the Economy subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette introduced the bill on March 15, 2011, with 32 original cosponsors listed in the bill text.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and six days later to the Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy.
73 members cosponsored the bill — 72 Democrats and 1 Republican — but the bill received no further action, no markup, and no vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas drillers and their chemical suppliers are better off: they kept the 2005 Safe Drinking Water Act exemption and their chemical disclosure practices stayed voluntary and state-by-state, while residents near wells got no new right to know what is injected underground.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas drillers and chemical suppliers

for.name: Rep. Diana DeGette
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the fracking exemption from the Safe Drinking Water Act and require chemical disclosure.

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it sat in his committee and its Environment and the Economy subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas drillers and service companies
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal oversight of hydraulic fracturing and disclosure of fracturing chemicals, and lobbied against comparable FRAC Act bills.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 72 of 73 cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican — and the Republican-controlled committee took no action.

industries.note: The bill removes the 2005 exemption that lets them inject fracturing fluids without Safe Drinking Water Act oversight, a carve-out known as the 'Halliburton loophole.' Operators would face federal injection controls and mandatory chemical reporting on every well.

industries.industry: Fracturing chemical suppliers and service companies
industries.note: They would have to report chemical constituents, volumes, and CAS numbers before and after each job, and hand over trade secret identities in medical emergencies. The bill does shield proprietary formulas from blanket public disclosure, but the emergency-disclosure rule and public posting of constituents cut into the confidentiality they now enjoy.

The bill writes fracturing for geothermal production into the Safe Drinking Water Act alongside oil and gas, so geothermal operators lose the same exemption, though the practical burden is small next to oil and gas.
